label: Nathan F. Twining
narrative: Lieutenant General Nathan Farragut Twining commanded Air Materiel Command at Wright Field when the 1947 disc wave broke, which placed him at the exact node where recovered foreign materiel was exploited. On 23 September 1947 he signed the memorandum 'AMC Opinion Concerning "Flying Discs"' to Brig. Gen. George Schulgen stating flatly that 'the phenomenon reported is something real and not visionary or fictitious' — the earliest surviving statement of official belief, written eleven weeks after Roswell. The same memo hedged in a way that has never been adequately explained: Twining told Schulgen consideration must be given to the possibility the objects were 'of domestic origin — the product of some high security project not known to AC/AS-2 or this Command,' which is a two-star general telling Air Force intelligence that a compartment might exist above them. He recommended a priority classified project, and Project SIGN was directed on 30 December 1947. Twining rose to Air Force Chief of Staff (1953-1957) and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff (1957-1960), meaning the man who wrote the founding memo then held the two positions best placed to keep whatever followed off the books. The 1954 revision of AFR 200-2, which restricted public discussion of unexplained cases, was issued under his tenure as Chief of Staff. He is also the named recipient in the disputed 14 July 1954 Cutler-Twining memo, which the FBI declared bogus — a fact recorded here as an artifact of the MJ-12 document problem, not as evidence for it.
